import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Borromean rings

The Borromean rings are the three-component link `L6a4`: three simple closed curves in
$\mathbb{R}^3$ that are linked, but such that any two of them are unlinked. Here they are
modelled by the standard realization as three mutually perpendicular ellipses.

A classical theorem (Lindström–Zetterström, and Freedman–Skora for arbitrary Brunnian links) says
that the Borromean rings cannot be formed from three round circles. In the other direction,
Matthew Cook conjectured that *any* three unknotted simple closed curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that
are not all circles can be arranged, by rigid motions of the individual components without
scaling, to form the Borromean rings. Howards proved this for polygonal unknots when scaling is
allowed (and, without scaling, when at least two of the polygons are planar), but also stated the
opposite conjecture, based on a candidate counterexample suggested by Jason Cantarella.

The Wikipedia list of unsolved problems asks:
*are there three unknotted space curves, not all three circles, which cannot be arranged to form
this link?*

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Borromean rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borromean_rings)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [H. N. Howards, *Forming the Borromean rings out of arbitrary polygonal unknots*,
  arXiv:1406.3370](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3370)
- B. Lindström, H.-O. Zetterström, *Borromean circles are impossible*,
  Amer. Math. Monthly 98 (1991), 340–341.
- M. H. Freedman, R. Skora, *Strange actions of groups on spheres*,
  J. Differential Geom. 25 (1987), 75–98.
-/

blocks.docstring:
Two subsets `A`, `B` of `ℝ³` are **ambient isotopic** if there is a continuous family
`H t` (`t ∈ [0, 1]`) of homeomorphisms of `ℝ³` that starts at the identity and whose final
homeomorphism `H 1` maps `A` onto `B`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: ContinuousMap.Homotopy / HomotopyEquiv (homotopies of maps, not ambient isotopies of subsets); Homeomorph alone (would not capture isotopy to the identity).
justification.name: BorromeanRings.AmbientIsotopic
justification.why_needed: Link equivalence (ambient isotopy in ℝ³) is not in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib. Defined as a family `H : I → ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³` of homeomorphisms, jointly continuous in (t, x), with `H 0 = id` and `H 1 '' A = B`.

blocks.name: AmbientIsotopic
blocks.text:
/-- Two subsets `A`, `B` of `ℝ³` are **ambient isotopic** if there is a continuous family
`H t` (`t ∈ [0, 1]`) of homeomorphisms of `ℝ³` that starts at the identity and whose final
homeomorphism `H 1` maps `A` onto `B`. -/
def AmbientIsotopic (A B : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ H : I → ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³,
    Continuous (fun p : I × ℝ³ => H p.1 p.2) ∧ H 0 = Homeomorph.refl ℝ³ ∧ H 1 '' A = B

blocks.code:
@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem ambientIsotopic_refl (A : Set ℝ³) : AmbientIsotopic A A :=
  ⟨fun _ => Homeomorph.refl ℝ³, continuous_snd, rfl, Set.image_id A⟩
blocks.name: ambientIsotopic_refl
blocks.text:
@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem ambientIsotopic_refl (A : Set ℝ³) : AmbientIsotopic A A :=
  ⟨fun _ => Homeomorph.refl ℝ³, continuous_snd, rfl, Set.image_id A⟩

blocks.code:
def IsRoundCircle (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ (c n : ℝ³) (r : ℝ), n ≠ 0 ∧ 0 < r ∧ K = {x | dist x c = r ∧ inner ℝ (x - c) n = 0}
blocks.docstring:
A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is a **round circle** if it is the set of points of some plane at a
fixed positive distance `r` from a centre `c` lying in that plane. The plane is described by the
centre `c` and a nonzero normal vector `n`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: EuclideanGeometry.Sphere and Metric.sphere (spheres, not circles in ℝ³); `Circle` (the unit circle in ℂ, not a subset of ℝ³); SquarePacking.Circle (a disc in ℝ²).
justification.name: BorromeanRings.IsRoundCircle
justification.why_needed: Needed for both 'unknotted' (ambient isotopic to a round circle) and 'not all three circles'. Defined as `Metric.sphere c r ∩ P` with `0 < r`, `c ∈ P`, `P` an affine subspace of ℝ³ with `finrank P.direction = 2`.

blocks.name: IsRoundCircle

blocks.code:
@[category test, AMS 51 57]
theorem isRoundCircle_unitCircle : IsRoundCircle {p : ℝ³ | p 2 = 0 ∧ ‖p‖ = 1} := by
  refine ⟨0, EuclideanSpace.single 2 1, 1, ?_, one_pos, ?_⟩
  · simp
  · ext x
    simp [EuclideanSpace.inner_single_right, and_comm]
blocks.docstring: The unit circle in the $xy$-plane is a round circle.
blocks.name: isRoundCircle_unitCircle
blocks.text:
/-- The unit circle in the $xy$-plane is a round circle. -/
@[category test, AMS 51 57]
theorem isRoundCircle_unitCircle : IsRoundCircle {p : ℝ³ | p 2 = 0 ∧ ‖p‖ = 1} := by
  refine ⟨0, EuclideanSpace.single 2 1, 1, ?_, one_pos, ?_⟩
  · simp
  · ext x
    simp [EuclideanSpace.inner_single_right, and_comm]

blocks.code:
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ C, IsRoundCircle C ∧ AmbientIsotopic K C
blocks.docstring:
A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an **unknotted space curve** (an unknot) if it is ambient isotopic to
a round circle. Such a set is automatically a tame simple closed curve, i.e. the image of a
topological embedding of the circle.

justification.closest_existing_considered: IsEmbedding γ for γ : Circle → ℝ³ (used in InscribedSquare.lean) gives simple closed curves but says nothing about being unknotted.
justification.name: BorromeanRings.IsUnknot
justification.why_needed: 'Unknotted space curve': a subset of ℝ³ ambient isotopic to a round circle (hence automatically a tame simple closed curve).

blocks.name: IsUnknot
blocks.text:
/-- A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an **unknotted space curve** (an unknot) if it is ambient isotopic to
a round circle. Such a set is automatically a tame simple closed curve, i.e. the image of a
topological embedding of the circle. -/
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ C, IsRoundCircle C ∧ AmbientIsotopic K C

blocks.code:
@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem IsRoundCircle.isUnknot {K : Set ℝ³} (hK : IsRoundCircle K) : IsUnknot K :=
  ⟨K, hK, ambientIsotopic_refl K⟩
blocks.name: IsRoundCircle.isUnknot
blocks.text:
@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem IsRoundCircle.isUnknot {K : Set ℝ³} (hK : IsRoundCircle K) : IsUnknot K :=
  ⟨K, hK, ambientIsotopic_refl K⟩

blocks.code: def ellipse₁ : Set ℝ³ := {p | p 0 ^ 2 / 4 + p 1 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ p 2 = 0}
blocks.docstring: The ellipse $x^2 / 4 + y^2 = 1$ in the plane $z = 0$.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Nothing in Mathlib or the repo models any specific link or link diagram.
justification.name: BorromeanRings.ellipse₁ / ellipse₂ / ellipse₃ / borromeanRings
justification.why_needed: A concrete representative of the link L6a4 is needed to say 'this link'. Used the standard realization by three mutually perpendicular ellipses with semi-axes 2 and 1 (x²/4+y²=1 in z=0, y²/4+z²=1 in x=0, z²/4+x²=1 in y=0); the pairwise disk-intersection pattern (crossed arcs, one with endpoints on the boundary curve, one with endpoints interior) is the pattern Howards (arXiv:1406.3370) notes characterizes the Borromean rings, and the Wikipedia article states that ellipses (and perpendicular golden rectangles) realize them. Pairwise disjointness of the three ellipses is proved as API lemmas.

blocks.code: def borromeanRings : Set ℝ³ := ellipse₁ ∪ ellipse₂ ∪ ellipse₃
blocks.docstring:
The standard **Borromean rings**: the union of the three mutually perpendicular ellipses
`ellipse₁`, `ellipse₂`, `ellipse₃`, each with semi-axes `2` and `1`. The short axis of each
ellipse pierces the flat disk bounded by the next one (`ellipse₁` pierces the disk of `ellipse₂`
at $(0, \pm 1, 0)$, `ellipse₂` pierces the disk of `ellipse₃` at $(0, 0, \pm 1)$, and `ellipse₃`
pierces the disk of `ellipse₁` at $(\pm 1, 0, 0)$), while the long axis of each ellipse misses
the disk of the previous one. This is the configuration of the three golden rectangles inscribed
in a regular icosahedron, and it is the link `L6a4` (Alexander–Briggs `6³₂`).

blocks.docstring:
Three subsets `K₁`, `K₂`, `K₃` of `ℝ³` **form the Borromean rings** if they are pairwise
disjoint and their union is ambient isotopic to the standard Borromean rings `borromeanRings`.

justification.name: BorromeanRings.FormBorromeanRings
justification.why_needed: 'Form this link': three subsets of ℝ³ are pairwise disjoint and their union is ambient isotopic to `borromeanRings`.

blocks.name: FormBorromeanRings
blocks.text:
/-- Three subsets `K₁`, `K₂`, `K₃` of `ℝ³` **form the Borromean rings** if they are pairwise
disjoint and their union is ambient isotopic to the standard Borromean rings `borromeanRings`. -/
def FormBorromeanRings (K₁ K₂ K₃ : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  Disjoint K₁ K₂ ∧ Disjoint K₂ K₃ ∧ Disjoint K₁ K₃ ∧
    AmbientIsotopic (K₁ ∪ K₂ ∪ K₃) borromeanRings

blocks.code:
@[category test, AMS 51 57]
theorem formBorromeanRings_ellipses : FormBorromeanRings ellipse₁ ellipse₂ ellipse₃ :=
  ⟨disjoint_ellipse₁_ellipse₂, disjoint_ellipse₂_ellipse₃, disjoint_ellipse₁_ellipse₃,
    ambientIsotopic_refl _⟩
blocks.name: formBorromeanRings_ellipses

@[category research open, AMS 51 57]
theorem borromean_rings :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ K₁ K₂ K₃ : Set ℝ³, IsUnknot K₁ ∧ IsUnknot K₂ ∧ IsUnknot K₃ ∧
      ¬ (IsRoundCircle K₁ ∧ IsRoundCircle K₂ ∧ IsRoundCircle K₃) ∧
      ¬ ∃ σ₁ σ₂ σ₃ : ℝ³ ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] ℝ³, FormBorromeanRings (σ₁ '' K₁) (σ₂ '' K₂) (σ₃ '' K₃) := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
**Borromean rings from arbitrary unknots.**
Are there three unknotted space curves $K_1, K_2, K_3 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$, not all three
round circles, which cannot be arranged to form the Borromean rings?

Here "arranged" means that each curve $K_i$ is moved individually by a rigid motion of
$\mathbb{R}^3$, i.e. a Euclidean isometry $\sigma_i$ (a composition of translations, rotations
and reflections), without any scaling. The moved curves $\sigma_1(K_1), \sigma_2(K_2),
\sigma_3(K_3)$ form the Borromean rings when they are pairwise disjoint and their union is
ambient isotopic to the standard Borromean rings. The three curves need not be distinct or
congruent.

A positive answer is the conjecture of Howards (arXiv:1406.3370, Section 3, based on a candidate
counterexample of Cantarella); a negative answer is the conjecture of Matthew Cook
(arXiv:1406.3370, Conjecture 1.1) that any three unknotted simple closed curves in space, not all
circles, can be combined without scaling to form the Borromean rings. Howards notes that allowing
scaling of the components could change the answer; scaling is not allowed here.
blocks.name: borromean_rings

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no question (negation of Matthew Cook's conjecture, Howards arXiv:1406.3370 Conj. 1.1; Cook conjectures 'no', Howards conjectures 'yes' via Cantarella's candidate counterexample), so it is `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ K₁ K₂ K₃ ...`; 'unknotted space curves' are simple closed curves in ℝ³ each ambient-isotopic to a round circle, 'not all three circles' means at least one is not a round Euclidean circle (the three curves need not be congruent), 'arranged' means applying a rigid motion (Euclidean isometry) to each component individually WITHOUT scaling — the article says explicitly 'combined without scaling' and Howards notes the scaling nuance may decide truth (the scaling-allowed form and Howards's weakened planar-curves form are subordinate variants the statement does not itself pose) — and 'form this link' means the moved curves are pairwise disjoint and their union is ambient-isotopic in ℝ³ to the standard Borromean rings L6a4.
claims.reviewer_why: c03's declaration is used essentially verbatim: `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ K₁ K₂ K₃ : Set ℝ³, IsUnknot … ∧ ¬(all three IsRoundCircle) ∧ ¬∃ σ₁ σ₂ σ₃ : ℝ³ ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] ℝ³, FormBorromeanRings (σᵢ '' Kᵢ)`. It follows the table's reading exactly (rigid motion = Euclidean isometry applied per component, no scaling; unknot = ambient isotopic to a round circle; form the link = pairwise disjoint with union ambient isotopic to a concrete L6a4 model), uses the repo's scoped `ℝ³` notation and the `PompeiuProblem` precedent `AffineIsometryEquiv` for rigid motions, and proves disjointness of its model. I verified by hand that its three perpendicular ellipses (semi-axes 2,1) have the cyclic piercing pattern of the icosahedral golden-rectangle realization, i.e. are the Borromean rings. Edits: swapped in c01's simpler normal-vector `IsRoundCircle` together with its proven unit-circle test lemma, added the missing `AMS` tags on c03's API/test lemmas (every API/test statement in the repo carries one), removed c03's extra `research solved` companion theorem (not a slot), and expanded the theorem docstring to state the isometry/scaling reading and both conjectures. c01/c02/c04/c06/c07 were equally faithful (all E(3), correct models, correct isotopy) but were stylistically weaker (local macro / abbrev instead of the repo's `ℝ³` notation, parametrised curves adding an unnecessary `IsEmbedding` layer, or no API tests). c05 and c08 are faithful under the alternative SE(3) reading (orientation-preserving only), which departs from the table's specified 'Euclidean isometry' reading.

context:
In mathematics, the Borromean rings are three simple closed curves in three-dimensional space that are topologically linked and cannot be separated from each other, but that break apart into two unknotted and unlinked loops when any one of the three is cut or removed. Most commonly, these rings are drawn as three circles in the plane, in the pattern of a Venn diagram, alternatingly crossing over and under each other at the points where they cross. Other triples of curves are said to form the Borromean rings as long as they are topologically equivalent to the curves depicted in this drawing.
The Borromean rings are named after the Italian House of Borromeo, who used the circular form of these rings as an element of their coat of arms, but designs based on the Borromean rings have been used in many cultures, including by the Norsemen and in Japan. They have been used in Christian symbolism as a sign of the Trinity, and in modern commerce as the logo of Ballantine beer, giving them the alternative name Ballantine rings. Physical instances of the Borromean rings have been made from linked DNA or other molecules, and they have analogues in the Efimov state and Borromean nuclei, both of which have three components bound to each other although no two of them are bound.
Geometrically, the Borromean rings may be realized by linked ellipses, or (using the vertices of a regular icosahedron) by linked golden rectangles. It is impossible to realize them using circles in three-dimensional

decomposition_objections.text: None. The single-slot decomposition is appropriate. One remark: the notes say 'rigid motion (Euclidean isometry)'; the two phrases can differ (proper rigid motions vs. all isometries including reflections). I followed the parenthetical (all isometries) and recorded this as a modeling decision.

/-!
# Borromean rings

The Borromean rings are the three-component link `L6a4`: three simple closed curves in
$\mathbb{R}^3$ that are linked, but such that any two of them are unlinked. Here they are
modelled by the standard realization as three mutually perpendicular ellipses.

A classical theorem (Lindström–Zetterström, and Freedman–Skora for arbitrary Brunnian links) says
that the Borromean rings cannot be formed from three round circles. In the other direction,
Matthew Cook conjectured that *any* three unknotted simple closed curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that
are not all circles can be arranged, by rigid motions of the individual components without
scaling, to form the Borromean rings. Howards proved this for polygonal unknots when scaling is
allowed (and, without scaling, when at least two of the polygons are planar), but also stated the
opposite conjecture, based on a candidate counterexample suggested by Jason Cantarella.

The Wikipedia list of unsolved problems asks:
*are there three unknotted space curves, not all three circles, which cannot be arranged to form
this link?*

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Borromean rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borromean_rings)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [H. N. Howards, *Forming the Borromean rings out of arbitrary polygonal unknots*,
  arXiv:1406.3370](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3370)
- B. Lindström, H.-O. Zetterström, *Borromean circles are impossible*,
  Amer. Math. Monthly 98 (1991), 340–341.
- M. H. Freedman, R. Skora, *Strange actions of groups on spheres*,
  J. Differential Geom. 25 (1987), 75–98.
-/

open scoped EuclideanGeometry unitInterval

namespace BorromeanRings

/-- Two subsets `A`, `B` of `ℝ³` are **ambient isotopic** if there is a continuous family
`H t` (`t ∈ [0, 1]`) of homeomorphisms of `ℝ³` that starts at the identity and whose final
homeomorphism `H 1` maps `A` onto `B`. -/
def AmbientIsotopic (A B : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ H : I → ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³,
    Continuous (fun p : I × ℝ³ => H p.1 p.2) ∧ H 0 = Homeomorph.refl ℝ³ ∧ H 1 '' A = B

@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem ambientIsotopic_refl (A : Set ℝ³) : AmbientIsotopic A A :=
  ⟨fun _ => Homeomorph.refl ℝ³, continuous_snd, rfl, Set.image_id A⟩

/-- A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is a **round circle** if it is the set of points of some plane at a
fixed positive distance `r` from a centre `c` lying in that plane. The plane is described by the
centre `c` and a nonzero normal vector `n`. -/
def IsRoundCircle (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ (c n : ℝ³) (r : ℝ), n ≠ 0 ∧ 0 < r ∧ K = {x | dist x c = r ∧ inner ℝ (x - c) n = 0}

/-- The unit circle in the $xy$-plane is a round circle. -/
@[category test, AMS 51 57]
theorem isRoundCircle_unitCircle : IsRoundCircle {p : ℝ³ | p 2 = 0 ∧ ‖p‖ = 1} := by
  refine ⟨0, EuclideanSpace.single 2 1, 1, ?_, one_pos, ?_⟩
  · simp
  · ext x
    simp [EuclideanSpace.inner_single_right, and_comm]

/-- A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an **unknotted space curve** (an unknot) if it is ambient isotopic to
a round circle. Such a set is automatically a tame simple closed curve, i.e. the image of a
topological embedding of the circle. -/
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ C, IsRoundCircle C ∧ AmbientIsotopic K C

@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem IsRoundCircle.isUnknot {K : Set ℝ³} (hK : IsRoundCircle K) : IsUnknot K :=
  ⟨K, hK, ambientIsotopic_refl K⟩

/-- The ellipse $x^2 / 4 + y^2 = 1$ in the plane $z = 0$. -/
def ellipse₁ : Set ℝ³ := {p | p 0 ^ 2 / 4 + p 1 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ p 2 = 0}

/-- The ellipse $y^2 / 4 + z^2 = 1$ in the plane $x = 0$. -/
def ellipse₂ : Set ℝ³ := {p | p 1 ^ 2 / 4 + p 2 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ p 0 = 0}

/-- The ellipse $z^2 / 4 + x^2 = 1$ in the plane $y = 0$. -/
def ellipse₃ : Set ℝ³ := {p | p 2 ^ 2 / 4 + p 0 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ p 1 = 0}

/-- The standard **Borromean rings**: the union of the three mutually perpendicular ellipses
`ellipse₁`, `ellipse₂`, `ellipse₃`, each with semi-axes `2` and `1`. The short axis of each
ellipse pierces the flat disk bounded by the next one (`ellipse₁` pierces the disk of `ellipse₂`
at $(0, \pm 1, 0)$, `ellipse₂` pierces the disk of `ellipse₃` at $(0, 0, \pm 1)$, and `ellipse₃`
pierces the disk of `ellipse₁` at $(\pm 1, 0, 0)$), while the long axis of each ellipse misses
the disk of the previous one. This is the configuration of the three golden rectangles inscribed
in a regular icosahedron, and it is the link `L6a4` (Alexander–Briggs `6³₂`). -/
def borromeanRings : Set ℝ³ := ellipse₁ ∪ ellipse₂ ∪ ellipse₃

@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem disjoint_ellipse₁_ellipse₂ : Disjoint ellipse₁ ellipse₂ := by
  rw [Set.disjoint_left]
  rintro p ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ ⟨h₃, h₄⟩
  rw [h₂] at h₃
  rw [h₄] at h₁
  linarith

@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem disjoint_ellipse₂_ellipse₃ : Disjoint ellipse₂ ellipse₃ := by
  rw [Set.disjoint_left]
  rintro p ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ ⟨h₃, h₄⟩
  rw [h₂] at h₃
  rw [h₄] at h₁
  linarith

@[category API, AMS 51 57]
theorem disjoint_ellipse₁_ellipse₃ : Disjoint ellipse₁ ellipse₃ := by
  rw [Set.disjoint_left]
  rintro p ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ ⟨h₃, h₄⟩
  rw [h₂] at h₃
  rw [h₄] at h₁
  linarith

/-- Three subsets `K₁`, `K₂`, `K₃` of `ℝ³` **form the Borromean rings** if they are pairwise
disjoint and their union is ambient isotopic to the standard Borromean rings `borromeanRings`. -/
def FormBorromeanRings (K₁ K₂ K₃ : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  Disjoint K₁ K₂ ∧ Disjoint K₂ K₃ ∧ Disjoint K₁ K₃ ∧
    AmbientIsotopic (K₁ ∪ K₂ ∪ K₃) borromeanRings

@[category test, AMS 51 57]
theorem formBorromeanRings_ellipses : FormBorromeanRings ellipse₁ ellipse₂ ellipse₃ :=
  ⟨disjoint_ellipse₁_ellipse₂, disjoint_ellipse₂_ellipse₃, disjoint_ellipse₁_ellipse₃,
    ambientIsotopic_refl _⟩

/--
**Borromean rings from arbitrary unknots.**
Are there three unknotted space curves $K_1, K_2, K_3 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$, not all three
round circles, which cannot be arranged to form the Borromean rings?

Here "arranged" means that each curve $K_i$ is moved individually by a rigid motion of
$\mathbb{R}^3$, i.e. a Euclidean isometry $\sigma_i$ (a composition of translations, rotations
and reflections), without any scaling. The moved curves $\sigma_1(K_1), \sigma_2(K_2),
\sigma_3(K_3)$ form the Borromean rings when they are pairwise disjoint and their union is
ambient isotopic to the standard Borromean rings. The three curves need not be distinct or
congruent.

A positive answer is the conjecture of Howards (arXiv:1406.3370, Section 3, based on a candidate
counterexample of Cantarella); a negative answer is the conjecture of Matthew Cook
(arXiv:1406.3370, Conjecture 1.1) that any three unknotted simple closed curves in space, not all
circles, can be combined without scaling to form the Borromean rings. Howards notes that allowing
scaling of the components could change the answer; scaling is not allowed here.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51 57]
theorem borromean_rings :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ K₁ K₂ K₃ : Set ℝ³, IsUnknot K₁ ∧ IsUnknot K₂ ∧ IsUnknot K₃ ∧
      ¬ (IsRoundCircle K₁ ∧ IsRoundCircle K₂ ∧ IsRoundCircle K₃) ∧
      ¬ ∃ σ₁ σ₂ σ₃ : ℝ³ ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] ℝ³, FormBorromeanRings (σ₁ '' K₁) (σ₂ '' K₂) (σ₃ '' K₃) := by
  sorry

end BorromeanRings

items: 'Arranged' = each component moved individually by an `AffineIsometryEquiv ℝ ℝ³ ℝ³` (a Euclidean isometry, following the decomposition notes and the repo precedent in PompeiuProblem.lean). This includes reflections as well as translations/rotations; for planar components (e.g. the circles in Cantarella's candidate) this makes no difference, but for a chiral space curve an orientation-preserving-only reading would be a slightly different (formally weaker-to-arrange) statement. No scaling is allowed, matching 'combined without scaling'.

'Unknotted space curve' is modelled as a subset of ℝ³ ambient isotopic to a round circle. This automatically makes the set a tame simple closed curve (so no separate `IsEmbedding` condition is imposed) and excludes wild curves, for which 'unknotted' is not meaningful.

Ambient isotopy is defined as a jointly continuous family of homeomorphisms of ℝ³ starting at the identity whose end map sends A onto B (the standard definition); the isotopy is required at the level of the union of the three curves, which is equivalent to a component-wise formulation (up to permuting components) since homeomorphisms preserve connected components, and the Borromean rings are unordered/unoriented and amphichiral so no orientation or ordering bookkeeping is needed.

The 'standard Borromean rings' is a concrete set: the union of three mutually perpendicular ellipses with semi-axes 2 and 1. Reviewers should check that this configuration is indeed L6a4 (each ellipse's long axis pierces the interior of the next one cyclically; pairwise disjointness is proved in the file).
'Not all three circles' is `¬ (IsRoundCircle K₁ ∧ IsRoundCircle K₂ ∧ IsRoundCircle K₃)`; the curves need not be congruent or distinct.
`answer(True)` corresponds to Howards's conjecture (such curves exist), `answer(False)` to Cook's conjecture; the docstring records both.

A `research solved` companion theorem `not_formBorromeanRings_of_isRoundCircle` (three round circles never form the Borromean rings; Lindström–Zetterström, Freedman–Skora) is included as a sanity variant motivating the 'not all circles' hypothesis; it is not one of the table's slots.
Category `research open`, AMS tags 51 (geometry) and 57 (manifolds and cell complexes, which includes knot theory).

reviewer_notes: All eight candidates compiled and state the same mathematical content; none has a quantifier, bound, or direction error. The single substantive divergence is 'rigid motion': six candidates allow all Euclidean isometries E(3) (translations, rotations, reflections), while c05 and c08 restrict to proper motions SE(3). The two readings are not equivalent in general (a mirror-reversed single component is a different shape unless the curve is planar/achiral as a shape), although Howards's local argument for Cantarella's candidate and Cook's conjecture are both insensitive to it. The source ('arranged'; Howards: 'rigid motions'/'rigid transformations of the components') is ambiguous; I followed the decomposition table ('rigid motion (Euclidean isometry)'), the usual geometric notion of congruence (which includes reflections), and the repo precedent `PompeiuProblem.RigidMotion := AffineIsometryEquiv`, and made the choice explicit in the theorem docstring. A reviewer preferring SE(3) can add a positive-determinant condition as in c08. Other modelling points, all standard and shared by every candidate: curves are subsets of ℝ³ (three copies of one curve are allowed, as in Cook's conjecture); 'unknotted' is ambient isotopy to a round circle (excludes wild curves); link equivalence is topological ambient isotopy of the union (fine since all curves are tame and the Borromean rings are amphichiral and unordered); the model of L6a4 is three concentric mutually perpendicular ellipses with semi-axes 2 and 1, whose cyclic piercing pattern I checked by hand (ellipse₁ pierces the disk of ellipse₂ at (0,±1,0), ellipse₂ that of ellipse₃ at (0,0,±1), ellipse₃ that of ellipse₁ at (±1,0,0); reverse intersections lie outside) — the icosahedral golden-rectangle configuration. Scaling of components is not allowed, per the article's 'combined without scaling' and Howards's remark that this nuance may decide the answer; the scaling-allowed and planar-curve variants are not stated. Final file compiles with only the `declaration uses 'sorry'` warning.
